# Can our sample represent the population?

## Class Survey

<br>

[Take the class survey](https://survey.60land.com/index.php/931648).

We will use the responses to compare sampling methods. As you answer, notice
how the questions and response options are written.

# Population to Sample

{{< include _population_pipeline.qmd >}}

## From Population to Survey Results

<br>

| Stage             | Question                      |
|-------------------|-------------------------------|
| Target population | Who do we want to understand? |
| Sampling frame    | Who could be selected?        |
| Planned sample    | Who did we try to select?     |
| Respondents       | Who actually answered?        |
| Final estimate    | What did we conclude?         |

::: notes
Ask where people could be left out between the population and the responses we receive.
:::

# Random vs Representative

## Random and Representative

# Sampling Methods

## How will we choose the sample?

<br>

Who can be selected, and how will we select them?

The selection rule determines the sampling method.

## [Probability Sampling]{.sr-only} {.w12-method-slide background-image="media/images/w12_go.jpeg" background-size="cover"}

<div class="w12-photo-label">
<h3>Probability Sampling</h3>
<p>Each unit has a known, nonzero chance of selection.</p>
</div>

## [Nonprobability Sampling]{.sr-only} {.w12-method-slide background-image="media/images/w12_spider.jpeg" background-size="cover"}

<div class="w12-photo-label w12-label-right">
<h3>Nonprobability Sampling</h3>
<p>Selection depends on access, judgment, or volunteers.</p>
</div>

## [Simple Random Sample]{.sr-only} {.w12-method-slide}

<a class="w12-coin-callback" href="https://shiny.60land.com/week06/coinflipper/"><img src="../week06/media/images/w6_shiny_coin_flip.png" alt="Week 6 coin-flip simulator callback"></a>
<img class="w12-bingo" src="media/images/w12_bingo.jpeg" alt="Bingo cage and numbered balls">
<div class="w12-plain-label">
<h3>Simple Random Sample</h3>
<p>Every unit has an equal chance of selection.</p>
</div>

::: notes
A simple random sample gives every possible sample of a given size the same
chance of selection. Use the bingo cage to illustrate drawing without choosing
particular numbers. The coin-flip image on the left links to the Week 6 example:
random selection can still produce a run or an uneven short sample.
:::

## [Convenience Sample]{.sr-only} {.w12-method-slide background-image="media/images/w12_marathon.jpeg" background-size="cover"}

<div class="w12-photo-label">
<h3>Convenience Sample</h3>
<p>Select people who are easy to reach.</p>
</div>

## [Stratified Sample]{.sr-only} {.w12-method-slide background-image="media/images/w12_red_white.jpeg" background-size="cover"}

<div class="w12-photo-label">
<h3>Stratified Sample</h3>
<p>Divide the population into groups, then randomly sample within each group.</p>
</div>

## [Quota Sample]{.sr-only} {.w12-method-slide background-image="media/images/w12_black_yellow.jpeg" background-size="cover"}

<div class="w12-photo-label">
<h3>Quota Sample</h3>
<p>Fill a target number from each group without random selection.</p>
</div>

## [Cluster, Judgment, and Snowball Samples]{.sr-only} {.w12-method-slide background-image="media/images/w12_larp.jpeg" background-size="cover"}

<div class="w12-photo-label w12-method-list">
<p><strong>Cluster:</strong> randomly select groups, then include their members.</p>
<p><strong>Judgment:</strong> select people for their relevant knowledge.</p>
<p><strong>Snowball:</strong> ask participants to refer other participants.</p>
</div>

# Sampling Lab

## Compare Samples

1. Choose an outcome and sample size in the [sampling app](https://shiny.60land.com/week12/samplinglab/).
2. Compare a random sample with a convenience sample.
3. Draw another sample. What changes?

Compare both the outcome and who is included with the full response pool.
Record your comparisons in Guided Notes 6.

::: notes
Keep the outcome and sample size fixed when comparing methods. Compare class
standing or attendance as well as the outcome. The response pool is our
reference for this exercise; it may not represent the whole university.
:::

# Survey Design

## Questions from Our Survey

<br>

Which questions were easy to answer? Which made you pause?

Look at the wording, the choices, and whether you could give the answer you wanted.

## Select One

![](media/images/survey-select-one.png){height=390px fig-alt="Class survey: class standing with four radio-button choices"}

Can everyone choose one answer that fits?


## Select All That Apply

![](media/images/survey-select-all.png){height=460px fig-alt="Class survey: majors with checkboxes for multiple selections"}

Would the percentages add to 100%?


## Ordered Response Scale

![](media/images/survey-ordered-scale.png){height=440px fig-alt="Class survey: confidence interpreting statistical results, from not at all to extremely confident"}

## Likert Scale

![](media/images/survey-likert.png){width=950px fig-alt="Class survey: agreement statements with strongly disagree through strongly agree choices"}

::: notes
Compare this agreement scale with the confidence question on the preceding
slide. Discuss what each response tells us and how the statements are worded.
:::


## Semantic Differential

![](media/images/survey-semantic-differential.png){width=950px fig-alt="Class survey: statistics rated between easy and difficult, useful and useless, concrete and abstract"}

What do the two ends of each scale mean?


## Numeric Scales Need Anchors

![](media/images/survey-numeric-slider.png){width=950px fig-alt="Class survey: a zero-to-100 slider for confidence explaining sampling bias"}

What does 0 mean? What does 100 mean?

::: notes
Discuss whether numerical bounds alone explain the scale. Compare with explicit
anchors: 0 = not confident at all; 50 = somewhat confident; 100 = completely
confident. These are discussion examples, not labels shown in the live question.
:::


## Constant Sum

![](media/images/survey-constant-sum.png){height=530px fig-alt="Class survey: allocate 100 points among six influences on success in class"}

::: notes
The total must equal 100. Ask what allocating more points to one item requires
students to do with the others.
:::


## Graphic Rating Scales

![](media/images/survey-graphic-faces.png){.w12-survey-faces fig-alt="Class survey: five faces from sad to happy for rating how coding in R feels"}

::: notes
Use the face scale students saw in the survey as the graphical rating example.
Discuss how the scale is presented and what the endpoints mean.
:::

## Drilldown Questions

<br>

::: {.callout-note title="Drilldown"}
Start broad, then narrow the choices.
:::

<br>

Better than forcing people through a giant pick list.

Example:

College -\> Department -\> Major

## Answer Categories in Our Survey

![](media/images/survey-age-options.png){height=360px fig-alt="Class survey: age categories 18 to 20, 20 to 22, and 22 to 24"}

Where would a 20-year-old fit? What about someone who is 25?

## Collectively Exhaustive vs Mutually Exclusive

:::: {.q-example}
::: {.q-title}
Question categories can fail in different ways
:::

::: {.q-col .left}
::: {.col-head}
Collectively Exhaustive
:::

::: {.prompt}
How old are you?
:::

- 18-20
- 20-22
- 22-24

::: {.prompt}
How old are you?
:::

- < 18
- 18-20
- 20-22
- 22-24
- 24+
:::

::: {.q-col .right}
::: {.col-head}
Mutually Exclusive
:::

::: {.prompt}
How old are you?
:::

- 18-20
- 21-22
- 23-24

::: {.prompt}
How old are you?
:::

- < 18
- 18-20
- 21-22
- 23-24
- 25+
:::

::: {.frame}
![](media/images/w12_birthday.jpeg){.food fig-alt="Birthday cake"}
:::

## Text Boxes

<br>

::: {.callout-tip title="Open text"}
Text boxes reveal categories the researcher did not anticipate.
:::

<br>

Example:

> What is something unique about you that a normal survey would not know to ask?

## From Text Boxes to Sampling

<br>

If someone writes:

> My obscure hobby is competitive speedcubing.

<br>

How would we sample that population?

::: {.callout-important title="Key link"}
Rare or niche populations often require judgment, cluster, or snowball sampling.
:::

# Bad Questions

## Leading Question

<br>

Bad:

> How much do you agree that this helpful course improves your analytical thinking?

<br>

Problem:

The wording pushes respondents toward a positive answer.

## Loaded Question

<br>

Bad:

> How often do you waste time using AI instead of thinking for yourself?

<br>

Problem:

The wording judges the respondent before they answer.

## Double-Barreled Question

<br>

Bad:

> The Shiny apps are easy to use and help me learn the material.

<br>

Problem:

This asks two questions at once.

## Assumption Question

<br>

Bad:

> How often do you use ChatGPT to complete your homework?

<br>

Problem:

It assumes the respondent uses ChatGPT.

## Better Question Flow

<br>

1.  Have you used ChatGPT or another AI assistant for homework?
2.  If yes, how often?
3.  If yes, for which tasks?
4.  What did you check yourself?

::: notes
Use this to connect back to responsible AI expectations from earlier homework.
:::

# Wrap Up

## What makes a survey good?

<br>

Survey quality depends on:

-   who could be selected
-   who was selected
-   who responded
-   what they were asked
-   whether the question measured what we think it measured

::: {.callout-tip .fragment title="Before trusting a survey result"}
Ask: who was in the frame, how were they sampled, who responded, and how was the question worded?
:::
